#9856. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9855. Small Language Models, Not Giant LLMs, Should Power the Next Generation of AI Agents

Source: arXiv:2506.02153, available under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Large language models (LLMs) are often praised for exhibiting near-human performance on a wide range of tasks and valued for their ability to hold a general conversation. The rise of agentic AI systems is, however, ushering in a mass of applications in which language models perform a small number of specialized tasks repetitively and with little variation.

Here we lay out the position that small language models (SLMs) are sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems, and are therefore the future of agentic AI. Our argumentation is grounded in the current level of capabilities exhibited by SLMs, the common architectures of agentic systems, and the economy of LM deployment. We further argue that in situations where general-purpose conversational abilities are essential, heterogeneous agentic systems (i.e., agents invoking multiple different models) are the natural choice. We discuss the potential barriers for the adoption of SLMs in agentic systems and outline a general LLM-to-SLM agent conversion algorithm.

Our position (The views and positions expressed in this paper are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of any entities they represent.), formulated as a value statement, highlights the significance of the operational and economic impact even a partial shift from LLMs to SLMs is to have on the AI agent industry. We aim to stimulate the discussion on the effective use of AI resources and hope to advance the efforts to lower the costs of AI of the present day. Calling for both contributions to and critique of our position, we commit to publishing all such correspondence at research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/slm-agents.

The deployment of agentic artificial intelligence is on a meteoric rise. Recent surveys show that more than a half of large IT enterprises are actively using AI agents, with 21% having adopted just within the last year [14]. Aside from the users, markets also see substantial economic value in AI agents: As of late 2024, the agentic AI sector had seen more than USD 2bn in startup funding, was valued at USD 5.2bn, and was expected to grow to nearly USD 200bn by 2034 [46, 51]. Put plainly, there is a growing expectation that AI agents will play a substantial role in the modern economy.

The core components powering most modern AI agents are (very) large language models [52, 48]. It is the LLMs that provide the foundational intelligence that enables agents to make strategic decisions about when and how to use available tools, control the flow of operations needed to complete tasks, and, if necessary, to break down complex tasks into manageable subtasks and to perform reasoning for action planning and problem-solving [52, 17]. A typical AI agent then simply communicates with a chosen LLM API endpoint by making requests to centralized cloud infrastructure that hosts these models [52].

LLM API endpoints are specifically designed to serve a large volume of diverse requests using one generalist LLM. This operational model is deeply ingrained in the industry. In fact, it forms the foundation of substantial capital investment in the hosting cloud infrastructure – estimated at USD 57bn [16]. It is anticipated that this operational model will remain the cornerstone of the industry and that the large initial investment will deliver returns comparable to traditional software and internet solutions within 3-4 years [57].

In this work, we recognize the dominance of the standard operational model but verbally challenge one of its aspects, namely the custom that the agents’ requests to access language intelligence are – in spite of their comparative simplicity – handled by singleton choices of generalist LLMs. We state (Section 2), argue (Section 3), and defend (Section 4) the position that the small, rather than large, language models are the future of agentic AI. We, however, recognize the business commitment and the now-legacy praxis that is the cause for the contrary state of the present (Section 5). In remedy, we provide an outline of a conversion algorithm for the migration of agentic applications from LLMs to SLMs (Section 6), and call for a wider discussion (Section 7). If needed to concretize our stance, we attach a set of short case studies estimating the potential extent of LLM-to-SLM replacement in selected popular open-source agents (Appendix B).

For the purpose of concretizing our position, we use the following working definitions:

We justify the wording of these definitions in Appendix A, but note that their choice has little bearing on the essence of our position. We note that as of 2025, we would be comfortable with considering most models below 10bn parameters in size to be SLMs.

We use the words agent and agentic system interchangeably, preferring the former when emphasizing the software with some agency as a whole (e.g., “as seen in popular coding agents”) and the latter when highlighting the systems aspect of the agentic application as a sum of its components (e.g., “not all LMs of an agentic system are replaceable by SLMs”). For brevity, we focus on LMs as the bedrock of agentic applications and do not explicitly consider vision-language models, although we note that our position and most of our arguments readily extend to vision-language models as well.

V1 principally sufficiently powerful to handle language modeling errands of agentic applications;

V2 inherently more operationally suitable for use in agentic systems than LLMs;

V3 necessarily more economical for the vast majority of LM uses in agentic systems than their general-purpose LLM counterparts by the virtue of their smaller size;

and that on the basis of items V1, V2 and V3 SLMs are the future of agentic AI.

The phrasing of our position is deliberate. In its statement, we wish to convey that the described future development is ultimately a necessary consequence of the differences between SLMs and LLMs if the natural priorities are followed. We do not make a recommendation or try to impose an obligation — we make a statement of what we see as a faithful reflection of the community’s values in this context.

We assert that the dominance of LLMs in the design of AI agents is both excessive and misaligned with the functional demands of most agentic use cases. While LLMs offer impressive generality and conversational fluency, the majority of agentic sub tasks in deployed agentic systems are repetitive, scoped, and non-conversational—calling for models that are efficient, predictable, and inexpensive. In this context, SLMs not only suffice, but are often preferable. They offer several advantages: lower latency, reduced memory and computational requirements, and significantly lower operational costs, all while maintaining adequate task performance in constrained domains.

Our position stems from a pragmatic view of language model usage patterns within agentic architectures. These systems typically decompose complex goals into modular sub-tasks, each of which can be reliably handled by specialized or fine-tuned SLMs. We argue that insisting on LLMs for all such tasks reflects a misallocation of computational resources—one that is economically inefficient and environmentally unsustainable at scale.

Moreover, in cases where general reasoning or open-domain dialogue is essential, we advocate for heterogeneous agentic systems, where SLMs are used by default and LLMs are invoked selectively and sparingly. This modular composition — combining the precision and efficiency of SLMs with the generality of LLMs — enables the construction of agents that are both cost-effective and capable.

Ultimately, we observe that shifting the paradigm from LLM-centric to SLM-first architectures represents to many not only a technical refinement but also a Humean moral ought. As the AI community grapples with rising infrastructure costs and environmental concerns, adopting and normalizing the use of SLMs in agentic workflows can play a crucial role in promoting responsible and sustainable AI deployment.

We support items V1, V2 and V3 by the following non-exclusive arguments.

A1 SLMs are sufficiently powerful to take the place of LLMs in agentic systems. This argument stands in support of item V1.

Over the past few years, the capabilities of small language models have advanced significantly. Although the LM scaling laws remain observed, the scaling curve between model size and capabilities is becoming increasingly steeper, implying that the capabilities of newer small language models are much closer to those of previous large language models. Indeed, recent advances show that well-designed small language models can meet or exceed the task performance previously attributed only to much larger models.

Extensive comparisons with large models have been conducted in the individual works cited below, but not all capabilities assessed by benchmarks are essential to their deployment in the agentic context. Here we highlight their aptitude for commonsense reasoning (an indicator of basic understanding), tool calling and code generation (both indicators of the ability to correctly communicate across the model→tool/code interface; see Figure 1; [77, 78]), and instruction following (ability to correctly respond back across the code←model interface; [83]). In each case, we also quote the efficiency increase if stated by the authors.

Note that on top of competitive off-the-shelf performance, the reasoning capabilities of SLMs can be enhanced by light-weight selective finetuning [45] or at inference time with self-consistency, verifier feedback, or tool augmentation — e.g., Toolformer (6.7bn) outperforms GPT-3 (175bn) via API use [65], and appropriately prompted language models rival directly applied LLMs on math problems [84].

In sum, with modern training, prompting, and agentic augmentation techniques, capability — not the parameter count — is the binding constraint. SLMs now supply sufficient reasoning power for a substantial portion of agentic invocations, making them not just viable, but comparatively more suitable than LLMs for modular and scalable agentic systems.

A2 SLMs are more economical than LLMs in agentic systems. This argument supports item V3.

Small models provide significant benefits in cost-efficiency, adaptability, and deployment flexibility. These advantages are specifically valuable in agentic workflows where specialization and iterative refinement are critical. Section 3.1 detailed a number of efficiency comparisons of the listed SLMs to relevant LLMs. Here we draw a more encompassing picture to support item A2.

Modular system design. The position outlined in [56] presents a thorough argument in favor of composite agentic systems. Here we note that the approach of leveraging several models of varying sizes aligns well with the real-world heterogeneity of agentic tasks and is already slowly being incorporated into major software development frameworks [28]. Furthermore, this newly discovered sense for modularity in the context of agents allows for the easy addition of new skills and the ability to adapt to changing requirements, and is consistent with the push for modularity in language model design [27, 12, 40].

The above-mentioned “Lego-like” composition of agentic intelligence—scaling out by adding small, specialized experts instead of scaling up monolithic models—yields systems that are cheaper, faster to debug, easier to deploy, and better aligned with the operational diversity of real-world agents. When combined with tool calling, caching, and fine-grained routing, SLM-first architectures appear to offer the best path forward for cost-effective, modular, and sustainable agentic AI.

A3 SLMs possess greater operational flexibility in comparison to LLMs. This argument stands in support of items V2 and V3.

Due to their small size and the associated reduction in pre-training and fine-tuning costs (Section 3.2), SLMs are inherently more flexible than their large counterparts when appearing in agentic systems. As such, it becomes much more affordable and practical to train, adapt, and deploy multiple specialized expert models for different agentic routines. This efficiency enables rapid iteration and adaptation, making it feasible to address evolving user needs, including supporting new behaviors, meeting new output formatting requirements, and complying with changing local regulation in selected markets [73, 41, 72].

One particularly notable and desirable consequence of SLM flexibility when put in place of LLMs is the ensuing democratization of agents. When more individuals and organizations can participate in developing language models with the aim for deployment in agentic systems, the aggregate population of agents is more likely to represent a more diverse range of perspectives and societal needs. This diversity can then help with reducing the risk of systemic biases and encourage competition and innovation. With more actors entering the field to create and refine models, the field will advance more rapidly [38].

A4 Agentic applications are interfaces to a limited subset of LM capabilities. This supports items V1 and V2.

An AI agent is essentially a heavily instructed and externally choreographed gateway to a language model featuring a human-computer interface and a selection of tools that, when engaged correctly, do something of utility [73]. From this perspective, the underlying large language model that was engineered to be a powerful generalist is through a set of tediously written prompts and meticulously orchestrated context management restricted to operate within a small section of its otherwise large pallet of skills. Thus, we argue that a SLM appropriately fine-tuned for the selected prompts would suffice while having the above-mentioned benefits of increased efficiency and greater flexibility.

It could be argued back that the careful interfacing with a generalist LLM is necessary for strong performance on the narrow task because of the LLM’s better understanding of the broader language and the world (item AV1). This is addressed in Section 4.1.

A5 Agentic interactions necessitate close behavioral alignment. This aligns with item V2.

A typical AI agent has frequent interactions with code, be it through LM tool calling or by returning output that is to be parsed by a piece of agentic code that makes the LM call [52]. It is essential for the success of these interactions that the generated tool call and the generated output conform to strict formatting requirements imposed on it by the order, typing, and nature of the tool’s parameters, and the expectation of the code invoking the LM, respectively. In such cases, it becomes unnecessary for the model to handle multiple different formats (e.g. JSON/XML/Python for tool calls and XML/YAML/Markdown/Latex for output [54]), as only one would be chosen for consistency across the agentic application. It is also undesirable for the model to make the occasional hallucinatory mistake and respond in a format different from that being expected by the “code parts” of the agentic system. It is because of this that the SLM trained with a single formatting decision enforced during its post-training or encouraged through additional fine-tuning at a low cost is preferable over a general-purpose LLM in the context of AI agents.

A6 Agentic systems naturally allow for heterogeneity in the selection of models that they use. This aligns with item V2.

A language model can itself be a tool called by another language model. Likewise, every time the agent’s code invokes a language model, it can, in principle, choose any language model. This is illustrated in Figure 1. We argue that incorporating multiple language models of different sizes and capabilities for queries or operations of different levels of complexity offers a natural way for the introduction of SLMs. In the context of Figure 1- Left, an LLM can be used for the model with the root agency, while a SLM could be used for the subordinate LM. In Figure 1- Right, all LMs could in principle be specialized SLMs: one for conversationality, another one for carrying out controller-defined language modeling tasks.

A7 Agentic interactions are a good source for data for future model improvement. This is fundamentally supportive of item V2.

As noted in Section 3.4, invocations of tools and language models during an agentic process are often accompanied by careful prompting that focuses the language model on delivering the narrow functionality that is required at the time. Each one of these invocations is itself a natural source of data for future improvement (under the necessary assumption that no non-retainable confidential data is being processed). A listener decorating the tool/model call interface can gather specialized instruction data that can later be used to produce a fine-tune an expert SLM and lower the cost of that call in the future (see logger in Figure 1). We argue that this avenue is enabled by the architecture of agents [52] and produces high-quality organic data (that can be further post-filtered by considering the overall success of the workflow), thus making the production of expert SLMs to stand in place of LLMs a natural step in agent deployment — not just an auxiliary effort.

The following significant alternative views have been expressed in the academic and popular literature.

AV1 Let T be a single task using general language and let L,S be a large and a small language model of the same generation, respectively. The performance of L on T will always trump that of S.

This alternative view disputes item V2 and rests on the following counter-arguments:

CA1 There is a non-negligible body of empirical evidence of the superiority of large language models in general language understanding over small language models of the same generation. LLMs acquire their language understanding capabilities in accordance with scaling laws [18]. Their larger scale then enables them to demonstrate better performance across a wide array of specialized natural language tasks, including text generation, translation, and reasoning, outperforming small models trained both (a) in the same general fashion and (b) from scratch specifically for these tasks [58]. It can then be said that to claim otherwise is to contradict the LM scaling laws [32, 31].

CA2 Moreover, recent studies also purport that LLMs possess a “semantic hub” mechanism, which has been hypothesized to enable them to integrate and abstract semantic information from various modalities and languages in a generalized manner [80]. If true, LLMs could be thought to generalize knowledge across languages and domains far more effectively than smaller models, which under the same study lack the capacity for the presence of such a hub [80]. It can then argued that while small language models may be efficient for narrowly defined or highly specialized tasks, their limited scale fundamentally restricts their ability to achieve the same level of general language understanding in these specialized as LLMs because of the lack of room for the internalization of complex abstractions.

A conclusion can be then drawn that LLM generalist models will always retain the advantage of universally better performance on language tasks, no matter how narrowly defined, over small language models of the same generation. This to be to their advantage over SLMs when deployed in agentic applications.

The above alternative view is the most popularly cited belief against the use of SLMs, even when only a narrow language task needs to be performed [2, 71, 30, 1].

We believe that item CA1 is too limited to attack item V2, namely because

A8 Popular scaling law studies assume the model architecture to be kept constant [32, 31] within the same generation, whereas the recent work on small language model training demonstrates that there are distinct performance benefits to considering different architectures for different model sizes [23, 9].

A9 The flexibility of small language models (Section 3.3) comes to the rescue. A small language model can be easily fine-tuned for the task T of item AV1 to perform to the desired level of reliability. This is unaccounted for in scaling law studies.

A10 Reasoning (or, more generally, test-time compute scaling; see Section 3.2) is significantly more affordable. A small language model, still retaining its benefits of greater cross-device agility can be reasonable expected to be scalable at inference time to the desired level of reliability.

We also believe that item CA2 is too arcane to attack item V2 because

A11 The utility of the purported “semantic hub” shows itself when tasks or inputs at hand to be processed by the LM are complex. However, advanced agentic systems are either designed in their entirety or at least actively prompted to perform decompositions of complex problems and inputs [52, 17]. Therefore, we argue to the contrary that invocations of small language models within agentic systems would be on appropriately broken-down into sub-tasks so simple that any general abstract understanding due to the hub would be of little utility.

AV2 The per-token inference cost benefit of the smallness of specialized SLMs in agentic applications is dwarfed by the economy of scale.

It could be argued that the analysis in item A2 that put forth in favor of item V3 was ignorant of the wider business of AI model deployment:

CA3 It is more difficult to fully utilize and properly balance the load for an expert SLM inference endpoint than it is for a generalist LLM endpoint [70, 25].

CA4 The costs of inference infrastructure setup combined with the costs of acquiring and retaining talent for its upkeep are often omitted in inference cost calculations but figure more prominently if the deployment of (S)LMs became the responsibility of the agent service developer. Early industrial reports point to considerable costs associated with these operations [39, 13, 67].

Acknowledgment. We acknowledge that item AV2 is a valid view, with the exact economical considerations being highly case-specific. We believe that the jury is still out on item AV2, but that several factors hint that item V3 might prevail:

A12 Recent improvements in inference scheduling and large inference system modularization offer unprecedented levels of inference system flexibility in monolithic computing clusters [85, 60, 50], countering the traditional stance expressed in item CA3.

A13 The most recent analyses on the set-up costs of inference infrastructure indicate a consistent falling trend due to underlying technological reasons [82, 4].

AV3 Both the agentic world utilizing SLMs and agentic world utilizing LLMs are equally possible worlds, but the “LLM agentic world” has a considerable head start in terms of deployment practice and optimization, and the industry inertia already funnels efforts into innovation solely in that direction.

Acknowledgment. We acknowledge item AV3 as a distinct possibility, but maintain the position that the weight of advantages described across items A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 and A7 can plausibily overturn the present state of affairs.

It would be prudent to ask oneself: If the items A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 and A7 are truly compelling, why do the ever newer generations of agents seemingly just perpetuate the status quo of using generalist LLMs?

We believe the following to be among the today’s main barriers to wide-spread adoption of SLMs:

B1 Large amounts of upfront investment in centralized LLM inference infrastructure. As detailed in Section 1, large capital bets have been made on the centralized LLM inference being the leading paradigm in providing AI services in the future. As such, the industry has been much quicker at building the tools and infrastructure to that end, omitting any considerations for the possibility that more decentralized SLM or on-device inference might be equally feasible in the near future.

B2 Use of generalist benchmarks in SLM training, design, and evaluation. It must be pointed out that much of the work on SLM design and development follows the tracks of LLM design, focusing on the same generalist benchmarks in their development [47, 61]. On this point, [23] notes that if one focuses solely on benchmarks measuring the agentic utility of agents, the studied SLMs easily outperform larger models.

B3 Lack of popular awareness. SLMs often do not receive the level of marketing intensity and press attention LLMs do, despite their better suitability in many industrial scenarios.

We note that items B1, B2 and B3 are practical hurdles and far from being fundamental flaws of the SLM technology in the context of agentic AI. With advanced inference scheduling systems such as Dynamo [24], item B1 is being reduced to a mere effect of inertia. item B2 is becoming increasingly recognized in the field [23, 37], and it would be natural for item B3 to fall once the economic benefits of SLM deployment in agentic applications (item A2) are better known. With the inertia of item B1 in particular, we do not endeavor to give a timeline for the retreat of these barriers or the popular adoption of SLMs.

The very nature of agentic applications enables them to eventually switch from using LLM generalists to using SLM specialists at many of their interfaces. In the following steps, we outline an algorithm that describes one possible way to carry out the change of the underlying model painlessly.

S1 Secure usage data collection. The initial step involves deploying instrumentation to log all non-HCI agent calls, capturing input prompts, output responses, contents of individual tool calls, and optionally latency metrics for a later targeted optimization. In terms of implementation, it is the recommended practice to set up encrypted logging pipelines with role-based access controls [55] and anonymize all data with respect to its origins before storage [74]. See logger in Figure 1 for an illustration.

S2 Data curation and filtering. Begin collecting data through the pipelines of item S1. Once a satisfactory amount of data has been collected (10k-100k examples being sufficient for fine-tuning of small models as a rule of thumb [5, 22]), it is necessary to remove any PII, PHI, or any other application-specific sensitive data that could cause a data leak across user accounts once used to produce a SLM specialist. Many typical varieties of sensitive data can be detected and masked or removed using popular automated tools for dataset preparation [64, 62]. Application specific inputs (e.g. legal or internal documents) can be often be automatically paraphrased to obfuscate named entities and numerical details without compromising the general information content [11, 79, 76].

S3 Task clustering. Employ unsupervised clustering techniques on the collected prompts and agent actions to identify recurring patterns of requests or internal agent operations [35, 42, 21]. These clusters help define candidate tasks for SLM specialization. The granularity of tasks will depend on the diversity of operations; common examples include intent recognition, data extraction, summarization of specific document types, or code generation with respect to tools available to the agent.

S4 SLM selection. For each identified task, select one or more candidate SLMs. Criteria for selection include the SLM’s inherent capabilities (e.g., instruction following, reasoning, context window size), its performance on relevant benchmarks for the task type, its licensing, and its deployment footprint (memory, computational requirements). Models of Section 3.2 serve as good starting candidates.

S5 Specialized SLM fine-tuning. For each selected task and corresponding SLM candidate, prepare a task-specific dataset from the curated data collected in items S2 and S3. Then, fine-tune the chosen SLMs on these specialized datasets. PEFT techniques such as LoRA [34] or QLoRA [20] can be leveraged to reduce computational costs and memory requirements associated with fine-tuning, making the process more accessible. Full fine-tuning can also be considered if resources permit and maximal adaptation is required. In some cases, it may be beneficial to use knowledge distillation, where the specialist SLM is trained to mimic the outputs of the more powerful generalist LLM on the task-specific dataset. This can help transfer some of the more nuanced capabilities of the LLM to the SLM.

S6 Iteration and refinement. One may retrain the SLMs and the router model periodically with new data to maintain performance and adapt to evolving usage patterns. This forms a continuous improvement loop, returning to item S2 or item S4 as appropriate.

The agentic AI industry is showing the signs of a promise to have a transformative effect on white collar work and beyond.

It is the view of the authors that any expense savings or improvements on the sustainability of AI infrastructure would act as a catalyst for this transformation, and that it is thus eminently desirable to explore all options for doing so.

We therefore call for both contributions to and critique of our position, to be directed to agents@nvidia.com, and commit to publishing all such correspondence at research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/slm-agents.

This appendix provides two justifications for the choice of definitions in Section 2.1.

It is desirable to have a definition of SLMs that meets three key criteria:

We find item WD1 to possess all three. Item WD2 is then phrased to complement the set of all language models.

To explore the distinction between small and large language models in the context of agentic AI, let us adopt the uncompromising lens of an extremalist, for whom intelligence must be either maximally small or maximally large.

Imagine a super-intelligent system spanning galactic scales, marshaling all available matter to optimize its computations. Such a system, while theoretically capable of addressing profound questions would face insurmountable physical constraints. The speed of light limits communication, with round-trip delays across a galaxy potentially spanning tens of thousands of years [63]. This latency precludes real-time coordination, fragmenting the system into loosely coupled components rather than a unified "mind". At cosmological scales, spanning millions or billions of light-years, communication delays could approach or exceed the universe’s age of 13.8 billion years [15]. Such a system, while vast, would be impractical for human-relevant applications, its computations unfolding over eons.

Conversely, consider an infinitely small intelligent system, reduced to the minimal substrate capable of computation. Such a system, akin to the simplest biological organisms, would lack the sensors, effectors, or computational capacity to meaningfully interact with its environment. Its intelligence would be constrained to rudimentary evolution, much like early life forms that emerged 3.5 billion years ago [66]. Yet, even in nature, scale varies dramatically: living organisms range from bacteria (hundreds of nanometers) to blue whales (up to 30 meters), the heaviest ones being limited by heat dissipation due to their high volume-to-surface ratio [26]. At the cosmic scale, all terrestrial life appears microscopic, suggesting that absolute size is less critical than functional adaptability.

Hereby: Humans, often regarded as a pinnacle of intelligence, offer a useful anchor for defining SLMs and LLMs. With a brain-to-body mass ratio surpassed only by small mammals like mice [49], humans balance computational efficiency with practical embodiment. SLMs, by analogy, are systems compact enough to run on personal devices, be trained with modest human interaction, or perform constrained, verifiable tasks. LLMs, in contrast, demand datacenter-scale infrastructure, organization-level training, and extensive validation, reflecting their computational load. The extremalist perspective hints at a profound truth: intelligence is not defined by size alone but by the balance of capability, efficiency, and context. For agentic workflows, SLMs may offer agility and accessibility, while LLMs provide depth at the cost of scale.

It is because of this apparent continuum that, if pressed to provide a definition of SLMs, we choose to anchor it in characteristics of a model that can be deployed in a distributed fashion with present-day technology and be interactive enough when engaging with a human to be of utility. Proceeding in such a way, the contemporary instances of the definition will evolve as the technology underpinning these models advances, making the definition sufficiently timeless to be practical.

This appendix assesses the potential extent of replacing large language model invocations with small language models in three popular open-source agents: MetaGPT, Open Operator, and Cradle. Each case study examines the use of LLMs, evaluates where SLMs may be viable replacements, and concludes with an estimated percentage of replaceable queries.

Purpose. MetaGPT is a multi-agent framework designed to emulate a software company. It assigns roles such as Product Manager, Architect, Engineer, and QA Engineer to collaboratively handle tasks including requirement drafting, system design, implementation, and testing.

SLMs would be well-suited for routine code generation and boilerplate tasks, as well as for producing structured responses based on predefined templates. However, they would require further fine-tuning data to reliably perform more complex tasks, such as architectural reasoning and adaptive planning or debugging, which would initially benefit from the broader contextual understanding and the generality of LLMs.

In the case of MetaGPT, we estimate that about 60% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

Purpose. Open Operator is a workflow automation agent enabling users to define behaviours of agents that can perform tasks like API calls, monitoring, and orchestration using tools and services.

SLMs would be well-suited for tasks such as simple command parsing and routing, as well as generating messages based on predefined templates. They could be meeting their limitations when dealing with more complex tasks that would require multi-step reasoning or the ability to maintain conversation flow and context over time—areas where LLMs would continue to offer significant advantages.

In the case of Open Operator, we estimate that about 40% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

Purpose. Cradle is designed for General Computer Control (GCC), enabling agents to operate GUI applications via screenshot input and simulated user interaction.

SLMs would be well-suited for handling repetitive GUI interaction workflows and the execution of pre-learned click sequences. However, they would face challenges when it comes to tasks involving dynamic GUI adaptation or unstructured error resolution, which would require a higher degree of contextual understanding typically provided by LLMs.

In the case of Cradle, we estimate that about 70% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

#9854. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9853. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#9852. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
