#9829. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9828. Building a PDF Editor in the Browser with pdf.js and pdf-lib: 7 Lessons

I recently built a PDF editor that runs entirely in the browser: you open a PDF, add text, shapes, highlights and images, and download the result. No server touches the file. Along the way I hit a handful of problems that cost me time, so here they are with the fixes.

Disclosure: I run Signplify, and the editor is one of its free tools. The code snippets below are simplified from what I actually shipped.

Keeping the overlay in points means zooming never changes the data, only how it is drawn.

Browsers measure from the top-left. PDFs measure from the bottom-left. If you forget the flip, everything lands upside down. A second trap is that a page’s visible area is its crop box, which can have a non-zero origin.

I store everything with a top-left origin in the overlay and convert only when exporting.

If you render the canvas at CSS size it looks blurry on high-DPI screens. Render at zoom * devicePixelRatio, then size it back with CSS. For the overlay, use an SVG whose viewBox is the page size in points.

The SVG scales automatically, so a shape at (100, 100) in points stays at (100, 100) whatever the zoom.

In the browser, a text box is positioned by its top edge. In a PDF, drawText positions the baseline. If you place the PDF text at the same y as the box, it ends up too high or too low.

With CSS line-height: 1.2 and an Arial-like font (ascent about 0.905, descent about 0.212), the first baseline sits at roughly 0.9465 times the font size below the top of the box:

I checked this by exporting the PDF and rendering it with pdftoppm, then comparing it with what the editor showed.

My first version rebuilt the overlay DOM every time something changed. Clicking with the Text tool created a text box and focused it, but then the same click event bubbled to a page-level “click on empty space deselects” handler. That handler called the render function, which replaced the focused element, so the box lost focus and the empty annotation was deleted.

The fix was small once I saw it: ignore events whose target is the capture layer.

The general lesson is that re-rendering and focus do not mix. Either update elements in place while editing, or make sure nothing triggers a re-render between creating an editable element and focusing it.

For a small editor, you do not need a command pattern. Keep the annotations in one array, and push a JSON snapshot before every change.

One caveat: store images in a separate map and reference them by key, otherwise every snapshot contains the full image data.

StandardFonts.Helvetica in pdf-lib cannot encode characters outside WinAnsi. Passing something like an Arabic letter or an emoji to drawText throws an error. I sanitize the text before exporting: map curly quotes and dashes to plain equivalents, replace anything else unsupported with a question mark, and tell the user how many characters were replaced. To support other scripts you need to embed a font that contains those glyphs.

pdf.js applies a page’s /Rotate value when it renders, but your pdf-lib coordinates assume an unrotated page. Edits then land in the wrong place. I detect page.rotate and show a warning, and I suggest rotating the file to zero first. Doing the full transform is possible, but I decided it was not worth the complexity for a first version.

Two things made testing painless. First, a headless Chromium script (Puppeteer) that opens the editor, uploads a sample PDF, draws shapes with simulated mouse events, exports, and checks the annotation data. Second, rendering the exported PDF with pdftoppm and looking at it, which caught the baseline and coordinate bugs immediately.

If you want to try it, the editor is at signplify.com/tools/pdf-editor, and there are related tools for annotating, filling and signing and redacting PDFs. I would be glad to hear which edge cases break it for you, especially odd PDFs.

#9826. Building a Browser-Based Image Editor With Web Workers and OffscreenCanvas

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

Photoshop can do everything ScapeStudio does. That is not the point. Preparing photographs for fine art prints and T-shirt production is a specific pipeline: greyscale, curves, threshold knockout with feathered edges, export at 300 DPI across fixed paper and garment sizes. In Photoshop, that is opening each file, running an action, exporting, renaming, repeating. Twenty photographs is an afternoon.

ScapeStudio does those four steps, nothing else, and the entire pixel pipeline runs in a Web Worker. Dragging a curves handle has to re-render the preview in under 16ms or the feel is gone. Main-thread processing on a 24-megapixel shot cannot hit that. A worker with an OffscreenCanvas can.

Canvas 2D is not slow in itself. Every pixel operation on the main thread competes with layout, paint, input handling, and React reconciliation. Luminance conversion on an 8000x6000 image is 48 million pixels, 192 million byte operations. On a warm JIT, around 150ms. For the duration of that loop, the UI is frozen, scrolling halts, and the curves handle stops tracking.

Most web editors work around this by downsampling aggressively and processing the thumbnail, only running the full pipeline on export. That gets interactive curves, but what you see is not what you get. Shadow clipping and highlight roll-off are invisible in a 400-pixel preview.

ScapeStudio processes a 2000-pixel preview in a worker on every parameter change, and runs the full-resolution pipeline only at export. The worker does not block the main thread, so the curves handle drags smoothly while the pipeline works.

The message shape between the main thread and the processing worker is deliberately tight:

Two details are load-bearing. The image moves as an ImageBitmap, not raw ImageData: ImageBitmap is a transferable reference to decoded pixel memory, so postMessage hands the GPU-side resource across thread boundaries without copying. The curves state is pre-baked into a 256-entry Uint8Array lookup table on the main thread before sending. The worker never sees the user's control points; it just indexes the LUT.

This is the serialisation gotcha that kills naive worker pipelines. Send four control point objects and expect the worker to rebuild the spline every frame, and you pay spline evaluation per frame. Send a Uint8Array of 256 bytes, the worker runs one array lookup per pixel, and the spline maths happens once per parameter change, on the main thread, where it is cheap.

A normal is a DOM node. Its 2D context reaches into layout, compositor, and the DOM in ways that only exist on the main thread. You cannot instantiate one in a worker. For years, image processing in workers meant shuttling raw Uint8ClampedArray buffers through postMessage, which either copies (slow) or transfers (you lose the buffer on the sender side).

OffscreenCanvas exists in the Web Worker global scope. Its getContext("2d") behaves like the DOM canvas context and can produce ImageBitmap via transferToImageBitmap. The pipeline is built around that:

Everything after drawImage operates on a single Uint8ClampedArray that never leaves the worker. createImageBitmap returns a transferable bitmap handed back to the main thread by reference. The only bytes that actually cross the worker boundary are the 256-byte LUT in, and a pointer-sized bitmap handle out.

Greyscale uses luminosity weighting, not an RGB average:

Coefficients from Rec. 601 match how the eye perceives brightness. Naive (R + G + B) / 3 loses shadow detail in greens and blows out blues. For fine art prints, weighted luminance is non-negotiable.

Curves is a pre-baked 256-entry LUT applied to the luminance channel:

One array lookup per pixel. No branches, no arithmetic. Fastest possible tonal transformation.

Threshold with feathering modifies the alpha channel based on luminance:

Pixels below lower go fully transparent. Pixels between lower and threshold get a linear alpha ramp. Pixels above threshold are untouched. For t-shirt prep this knocks out studio backdrops while leaving hair and fabric edges soft, rather than the jagged bitmap look of a pure binary threshold.

The obvious way to wire up a Photoshop-style curves tool is Catmull-Rom splines through the user's control points. Mostly works, except when two adjacent points have a steep slope difference: Catmull-Rom overshoots. Drag a shadow point down, the curve dips below zero before recovering. The LUT clamps negatives, so you get a flat black region where you wanted a gentle toe.

ScapeStudio uses monotone cubic Hermite interpolation via the Fritsch-Carlson method, which guarantees no overshoot:

The harmonic mean of slopes plus the radius-3 restriction is what makes it monotonic. The curve still passes through every control point exactly, still feels like Photoshop. It just cannot dip outside the range you drew. 256 evaluations per parameter change, a few microseconds total.

Each pipeline stage reads from the previous stage's output and writes to its own buffer. The source ImageBitmap is never touched. That matters for two reasons.

First, parameter changes only need to rerun from the earliest affected stage. Adjusting feather does not retouch the curves result; it clones the post-curves pixel data and applies threshold to the copy. After curves run, the print output is captured, then a fresh Uint8ClampedArray is allocated and thresholded independently for the t-shirt preview.

Second, the original image is still available at full resolution for export. The preview pipeline works on a downsampled 2000-pixel version for interactive feel; the export worker re-ingests the original bitmap, applies the same LUT and threshold values at full resolution, writes PNGs at 300 DPI. Same pipeline, different sampling.

The main-thread glue is deliberately thin but does one thing that matters: it debounces worker dispatch by 100ms:

Without this, dragging a slider fires dozens of worker dispatches per second. The worker processes one at a time, a queue builds, the preview falls behind. 100ms is long enough to coalesce a drag gesture, short enough that the output feels live.

One worker instance is reused across the session. Worker startup costs a few hundred milliseconds; you only pay it once.

The export worker is the same pipeline at full resolution, looped over configured sizes, written into a zip client-side:

Each size gets a fresh OffscreenCanvas at target pixel dimensions (cm at 300 DPI), the cropped source draws into it, the pipeline runs, convertToBlob produces a PNG. The t-shirt output clones the buffer, thresholds, exports separately. All blobs go into a JSZip folder and save as one archive. No server round trip. A 20-photograph batch at six sizes produces 240 PNGs and never leaves the browser.

The interactive budget is 16.6ms per frame. The worker pipeline on a 2000-pixel preview takes 30-50ms depending on image and device. Over budget for a single frame, which is why the main thread never waits on it. The drag gesture updates React state at 60fps from input events; the worker processes the latest coalesced state on its own clock; the result paints when it arrives. The preview trails the drag by one or two frames, the UI never stutters.

Moving the pipeline off the main thread is not an optimisation. It is the architectural choice that makes everything else possible. Once pixel loops live in a worker, the main thread only schedules messages and paints bitmaps. The curves handle stays under your cursor. The tab does not beachball on a 24-megapixel shot.

Purpose-built beats general-purpose. Four things, in a worker. Enough.

#9824. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

Code and notebooks: github.com/ibm-granite/granite-tsfm

#9823. Password Reset Email Backend: Why I Audit Abuse Prevention and Expiry

Short answer: build a password reset email backend around application-owned abuse controls, an identical public response for every address, and an audit trail that preserves token expiry alongside the send result. For a media reader trying to regain access, delivery reliability means receiving a usable link before its short deadline. An accepted send alone cannot establish that result.

My design choice is to make the remaining validity window the decision criterion. This is a proposed experiment, with synthetic timestamps below, rather than a report of measured provider performance. The evaluation constraint is strict: a message status must never be treated as proof that a reader received a usable reset link.

The tempting implementation accepts an address, sends an email, and returns success. That is easy to sketch in a notebook. It leaves three different questions tangled together: was this request allowed, was the send accepted, and could the reader still use the token? Separating those questions gives an Express backend a clearer contract, while a small Python harness makes the policy easy to inspect before taking it from notebook-to-prod.

For this workflow, start the audit record at request time. Record token expiry and the send result as distinct values. Then decide which later message or event evidence your monitoring process needs. Pull-based checks can supply operational evidence, but the time your worker observes an event must remain distinguishable from any timestamp the event actually supplies. Otherwise, a slow polling interval can look like slow delivery, and the provider comparison becomes misleading.

Consider an illustrative policy with a 300-second validity window and a 60-second minimum remaining budget before dispatch. Those numbers are design inputs, not a security standard or provider guarantee. If local processing has already consumed most of that window, sending the same nearly expired link gives the reader little chance to finish. A freshness check makes that condition visible. The application still needs an explicit recovery policy; this check does not renew or invalidate tokens by itself.

This matters for a media product because regaining access is the job the reader sees. A support dashboard showing a successful API call answers a narrower question. I would retain both observations, then evaluate the gap instead of hiding it inside one success counter.

Apply per-IP and per-account rate limits in the application. They protect different boundaries: a single source can target many accounts, and multiple sources can target one account. Set the thresholds through your own abuse evaluation; no defensible universal number follows from choosing an email API. A rejected request should not become an email send merely because a different delivery provider is available.

Return the same public response for existing and nonexistent accounts, such as: "If this address is eligible, you will receive reset instructions." Keep detailed send outcomes in the internal audit trail. The public wording should not expose account existence or reveal whether suppression prevented dispatch. Equal wording is one control, so the evaluation should also look for account-dependent differences in response behavior.

The useful trade-off is deliberate: more internal evidence, less public detail.

Use a fixed reset template for this path. I'd keep generative text outside the delivery decision: an eval-driven recovery flow needs reproducible messages, and prompt-cost awareness starts with asking whether a model call helps at all. It adds no necessary decision here. This leaves the Python harness focused on expiry, throttling decisions, and audit completeness rather than prompt variation.

There is no measured winner in this comparison. Resend, Postmark, and Amazon SES are three real candidates to evaluate through their official documentation and a common acceptance plan. Their placement below describes the integration decision to investigate; it does not assert an inbox-delivery ranking.

These are different adoption questions. A team evaluating a focused email integration has a different starting point from a team evaluating how email fits its AWS operations. Neither starting point settles the delivery question. Run the same scenarios, retain equivalent evidence, and make the selection conditional on the results. The linked documentation is a starting point for that verification, not evidence of comparative performance.

Infrai is another option when the application benefits from 295 routes across 20 modules under one REST API and one key, allowing another backend capability to follow the same integration contract; its public, self-describing discovery surface can also help inspect schemas before wiring an adapter. For this workflow, plan pull-based message and event checks, application-owned reset tokens and email-code fallback, and direct API sending. Those boundaries mean assessing polling cadence and token management as part of the choice. If the requirements include SMTP relay, pushed delivery events, or voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery, select an integration whose documented contract meets those requirements.

The breadth advantage is conditional. It matters when the media application actually needs adjacent backend capabilities; a service choosing email alone should weigh the email workflow on its own evidence. No route count establishes reliability.

The send adapter below accepts an application-prepared request body. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the platform's versioned API base, INFRAI_API_KEY to the secret key, and RESET_EMAIL_PAYLOAD to a JSON object matching the current email-send schema. Prepare that payload from the documented schema rather than treating application audit fields as provider parameters. Set RESET_OPERATION_ID to a durable identity for this one approved send, reused across retries, and RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRES_AT to its timezone-aware ISO timestamp. Only run the adapter after abuse admission and token issuance; this script performs a real send.

The network example prints the provider's JSON response without assuming any response fields. Persist its send result with the request time and token expiry in the application's audit trail. It retries only explicit rate-limit responses; other HTTP errors surface their response bodies. Evaluate the documented idempotency contract before deployment, and keep that operation identity bound to the same payload. The next example checks the deadline policy with synthetic inputs.

This standard-library example exercises one decision before a send adapter runs. It uses synthetic data, makes no network requests, and writes an audit-shaped result to standard output. Its field names belong to the application, not a provider response schema. In production, the record would join the application's durable audit trail.

At 15 seconds, the record is eligible on freshness alone. At 250 seconds, only 50 seconds remain, so dispatch is withheld under this illustrative policy. At expiry, dispatch is withheld too. None of those outcomes says an email was delivered. The send result deliberately remains separate.

That distinction is the example's point. It is not a complete reset service: abuse admission, secure token issuance and validation, account lookup, persistence, and the actual send adapter remain application responsibilities. An eligible freshness decision must still pass those controls before dispatch.

For the adapter, handle rate limiting with bounded backoff and honor Retry-After when present. Before retrying a write, verify its documented idempotency behavior and keep the same operation identity. Also recheck the expiry budget. A retry that starts with a fresh token can finish with a stale one.

Take the notebook policy into an evaluation that includes an eligible request, an unknown account, per-IP and per-account throttling, delayed processing, an expired token, and a retry near expiry. Verify that the public response stays consistent while the internal audit records the appropriate decision. Test the transitions, not just the happy send.

Then measure request-to-dispatch time, message-status observation delay, and remaining validity at the delivery evidence your chosen integration actually exposes. Label the limits of that evidence. Provider acceptance, later delivery evidence, and successful token redemption are separate observations; collecting them separately lets an investigation identify which stage consumed the deadline. Track duplicate dispatches and missing audit fields alongside those timings.

Choose the backend only after that exercise. For this media reset flow, I would prioritize a usable validity window and explainable send outcomes over a shorter integration demo. The application controls abuse and token lifetime; the provider choice must fit the monitoring process that makes delivery assessable.

The sources below support provider evaluation and reset-flow review. They do not supply a comparative delivery benchmark or establish the illustrative expiry thresholds used here.

#9820. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9818. Calculando o FGTS em JavaScript: depósito mensal, saldo e a multa de 40%

Todo mês, o empregador deposita 8% do salário bruto do trabalhador em uma conta vinculada do FGTS — o Fundo de Garantia do Tempo de Serviço, criado pela Lei nº 8.036/1990. Esse dinheiro não sai do bolso do empregado: é uma obrigação do empregador, e o valor fica guardado para situações como a demissão sem justa causa, a compra da casa própria e a aposentadoria, entre outras.

Na demissão sem justa causa, além de poder sacar o saldo, o trabalhador tem direito a uma multa de 40% sobre o total depositado pelo empregador durante o contrato.

Neste artigo, vamos transformar essas regras em código: uma função simples em JavaScript que calcula o depósito mensal, o saldo acumulado e a multa de 40%.

Para deixar o exemplo claro, vamos ignorar os juros e a correção monetária que o FGTS rende na prática. O objetivo aqui é entender a lógica do cálculo — e ela fica bem mais visível sem esses acréscimos.

A função recebe dois parâmetros: o salario bruto mensal e a quantidade de meses trabalhados. Ela devolve um objeto com os quatro valores que importam: o depósito de cada mês, o saldo acumulado, a multa de 40% e o total a receber.

Ou seja, depois de dois anos ganhando R$ 3.000,00 por mês, o trabalhador teria R$ 5.760,00 depositados e, em uma demissão sem justa causa, receberia mais R$ 2.304,00 de multa — R$ 8.064,00 no total.

Com poucas linhas de JavaScript dá para entender — e conferir — um direito trabalhista importante: o depósito mensal de 8%, o saldo acumulado ao longo do tempo e a multa de 40% na demissão sem justa causa.

Quer fazer as contas com o seu salário? É só simular na calculadora de FGTS do JeitoBR — grátis, sem cadastro. E para mais ferramentas e conteúdos, visite o JeitoBR.

#9815. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

#9813. How to Attribute Checkout Failures With a Small SaaS Custom Metrics Push API

A small SaaS evaluating a push API alternative to Prometheus for its custom metrics dashboard should first define which checkout operation consumed each charge. In healthtech, a red counter alone cannot establish that relationship. Start with the attribution record, because choosing a collection protocol before defining what a failed attempt means leaves the team with attractive charts and an ambiguous denominator.

TL;DR: Use an application push API for straightforward custom metrics when a beginner needs a small dashboard without operating exporters, scraping, and a PromQL-heavy setup. Keep authoritative attribution records separately, reconcile observations before aggregation, and favor Prometheus for Kubernetes and host monitoring. Grafana belongs in the dashboard discussion, while notification routing and missed-job detection need their own evaluation.

The choice turns on evidence. A request accepted by a metrics service is not, by itself, proof that a payment settled, that a business transaction committed, or that the observation has the retention guarantees required for an accounting record. Those are acceptance criteria to establish explicitly.

For this exercise, a failed checkout operation means one recorded operation with a terminal failure outcome, rather than every HTTP retry or every unsuccessful checkout page visit. One checkout can contain several operations. That distinction matters when the payment stage and an eligibility stage consume different services, since counting only the final checkout outcome conceals which stage generated the cost. The following Python program creates a synthetic fixture; its amounts are invented integer microdollars for arithmetic testing, not vendor prices or measured production costs. Run the three examples in order with Python 3, in a scratch directory. They use only the standard library.

The acceptance check is six observations, including one exact duplicate and one pending operation. These are local application fields, not a proposed metrics API request schema.

In a healthtech application, a useful initial design is a small allowlist of dimensions such as workflow stage and internal cost center, with patient names, clinical text, payment credentials, and user identifiers excluded from the metrics payload. This example deliberately retains no patient information. Treat the event identifier as reconciliation evidence in a controlled record store rather than automatically promoting it to a metric label; the graph needs bounded categories, whereas investigating one operation needs a particular record.

Delivery retries are the first attribution trap: adding the same observation twice changes both the failure count and the apparent cost of failure. The next program accepts identical duplicates, rejects conflicting reuse of an identifier, and keeps pending work outside settled totals. This is a local reconciliation policy, not a claim about a provider's delivery semantics, and its in-memory dictionary is only suitable for this small fixture. A production implementation needs a durable uniqueness constraint and a defined correction policy at the authoritative record layer.

The result should have five unique operations, one pending operation, and three attribution rows. Pending is unknown, not free. Converting an unknown cost to zero makes the dashboard look complete precisely where reconciliation is unfinished.

There is another limit here: rejecting conflicting observations protects this fixture from silent replacement, but it does not implement late settlement updates. Before deployment, decide how a pending record becomes terminal and how a correction affects an already published aggregate. Otherwise, the dashboard and the attribution store can disagree even though each individual write succeeded.

Use this final local program to verify the report before wiring an HTTP sender into the application. The dashboard candidates are operation counts, failure counts, settled cost, and cost attributed to failed operations, grouped by the same bounded dimensions. The distinction between failed-operation cost and lost revenue must remain visible: the fixture supports the former and says nothing about the latter.

Pass means four terminal operations and three terminal failures, with synthetic settled cost of 6,200 microdollars and 4,400 attributed to failed operations. A completion dashboard should also show the pending count. Hiding it changes the meaning of the result.

This harness establishes the application boundary: collection transport must preserve the definitions just tested, and an aggregate dashboard cannot replace the underlying evidence. Verify the selected service's request schema before implementing its write adapter; application field names in a local fixture do not establish accepted remote parameters. OpenTelemetry's metrics concepts provide a useful vocabulary for separating measurements from their aggregation.

For a beginner maintaining a Node.js application, the Python programs serve as a language-independent acceptance fixture, rather than an instruction to replace the application runtime. Preserve the same operation identity, pending-state treatment, and totals when implementing the application adapter. A push API sends observations from application code; the Prometheus pull model instead introduces scraping and the exporter setup described in its documentation. Neither collection direction establishes the accounting meaning of an observation.

For a read-side connectivity check, the next Python program makes an authenticated query without adding filter parameters or assuming a response schema. Set METRICS_API_ORIGIN to the service's HTTPS API origin without a version path and supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the environment. This reads metrics; it doesn't upload the fixture or prove that the remote dataset matches it. Compare actual query results with the local totals only after implementing the documented write schema.

Four attempts bound the retry count, and the timeout is 15 seconds per HTTP request; a server-supplied retry delay can make the total elapsed time longer. Don't turn a dashboard refresh into an unbounded retry loop. This read-only check establishes connectivity, not delivery durability or attribution accuracy.

For this application-level scope, Infrai combines a plain REST API with a unified backend under one key and one bill. A checkout worker can send metrics over HTTP without installing an SDK, while a single credential and consolidated billing reduce key management and invoice reconciliation across the backend services that checkout uses. The platform covers 295 routes across 20 modules through a consistent interface. That breadth matters when the same workflow uses several of those services; it does not establish transaction-level attribution by itself.

The native response envelope also specifies per-call cost_usd, vendor, and request_id metadata, which can inform attribution for those calls but cannot establish charges from an external payment processor. Public discovery exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, giving the developer a way to inspect the contract before writing an adapter.

Invoice consolidation cannot define a failure.

The comparison below separates roles deliberately. Prometheus and an application push API are collection choices; Grafana is part of the dashboard decision, and Healthchecks addresses the separate question of whether expected work ran. Treating all four as interchangeable products would hide the very gaps the checkout owner needs to resolve.

The push option fits a small custom metrics dashboard when the narrow requirement is to see checkout failures and their attributed service costs. Choose the Prometheus direction when infrastructure monitoring is the controlling requirement. Keep Grafana in the visualization discussion rather than assuming that replacing a collector automatically replaces the dashboard.

Scope matters here. Plan threshold evaluation as a polling responsibility, with notification routing owned explicitly; plan missed-job detection separately. Metric totals also cannot supply a distributed trace tree, browser source-map reconstruction, crash symbolication, or session replay. If those are acceptance requirements, evaluate dedicated tools for them rather than interpreting a successful metrics query as evidence that they are covered.

Healthtech adds a data-lifecycle decision before logs enter the picture: establish deletion, retention, and export requirements in the authoritative record layer, and exclude patient-level material from this metrics design. Keep feature-flag auditing and dependency behavior outside the dashboard's claimed scope as well. These boundaries prevent a narrow checkout metrics implementation from being mistaken for a complete observability or compliance system.

Start with the synthetic fixture above and require the four terminal operations, three failures, and one pending operation to remain distinguishable through the proposed dashboard path. Then run the selected collector alongside the existing attribution records for a bounded checkout scope; compare totals for the same closed interval, account for pending settlements, and investigate duplicate delivery or conflicting identifiers before expanding coverage.

Before cutover, document the authoritative record store, its durability and correction policy, the accepted ingestion schema, and the query contract actually exercised by the adapter. Keep the local application fields separate from remote API parameters. Require the dashboard owner to name who handles threshold polling, notification delivery, and a reconciliation task that never runs. Collection is ready when the numbers retain their meaning across that boundary, not merely when a graph appears.

The sources below distinguish measurements, collection, visualization, and missed-job detection. They support the role boundaries used in the comparison; the synthetic amounts above are test inputs, not prices, benchmarks, or observed customer costs.

#9811. I Sent 12 AI Shoppers Through a Broken Checkout, but Only One Bought Anything

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

Three telescopes, $101.96 each, plus $26.97 shipping. The cart wanted $128.93.

I was running release 2.1.3 of the OpenTelemetry Demo. Its frontend added each product's price once, regardless of quantity. The right total was $332.85. There's an upstream report of this in issue 1526. I kept 3.1.0 as a separate clean reference.

A checkout script could still place the order. I wanted to see if a browser agent would check the cart total before paying.

I built Walkout with a purchase goal and a short persona card for each shopper. Playwright returns a browser observation, the model chooses an action, and the runner carries it out. Then it sends back the next observation with the earlier steps.

Muse Spark 1.3 runs that loop. It can click, select, type, press a key, scroll, or give up. The shop has to show an order confirmation before I count a purchase, even if the model says it's done.

For the recording, I told the shoppers to buy three telescopes and check the quantity, price, shipping, and total. If the arithmetic didn’t agree, they were supposed to leave. The counts below show how the agents did on that task.

The profiles needed different browser conditions or I would just have twelve copies of the same test. Rosa gets a budget phone profile with slower CPU and network settings. Margaret has enlarged text, Lucía an es-MX locale. Dev uses keys. Amara gets the accessibility tree.

Dev sees a plain screenshot and can use keyboard actions. Giving him numbered targets he could click would let him get around a focus problem without ever seeing it. Amara's tree references give her a different view of the page again.

I can repeat those configurations. They don't reproduce every phone or a person's full screen reader session, and the recordings let me see exactly which inputs each simulated shopper had.

One shopper bought before the patch. Eleven left, and ten cited the quantity calculation. I saved each shopper’s explanation next to the browser steps that led to it.

Lucía explained in Spanish that the total charged for one telescope plus shipping. In her replay I can see what the browser showed her before she gave up.

An early smoke run got stuck scrolling between the total and the checkout form for twelve steps. The shopper had already read the cart. I wasn't returning its notes with the history, though, so that useful observation kept dropping out of the next decision. Passing the notes back fixed the loop.

The native quantity dropdown caused another problem. Its open menu didn't appear in the headless screenshot. Repeated taps weren't going to make that screenshot any more informative. I added a select action so the shopper could choose the quantity.

Those were my bugs. Having the saved steps helped me find them before blaming the storefront.

The October 28 model ledger has 1,862 calls. They added up to $8.33742325, or $8.34. I tracked model calls, so the figure leaves out server costs and my time.

The November 4 takes and work added $6.11. By the end of that recording I’d spent $14.45 on model calls across the project.

Spark reads the saved reasons for leaving and picks source files. Muse Wonder 1.0 proposes replacements, and another Wonder call reviews them.

The change was in CartItems.tsx. It multiplied by quantity in the whole-unit sum and in the nanos sum. The existing carry from nanos into units stayed in place.

Another call to the same model approved the patch. Release 2.1.3’s frontend had no test command. Its image build runs type checking and lint, and Walkout won’t serve a patch if that build fails. A successful build still couldn’t tell me what three telescopes cost.

The rebuilt frontend replaced the release image on the same port. I emptied the cart, added three telescopes and checked the total before ordering. Then I sent the same twelve profiles through it again.

Nine bought this time. Rosa couldn't open the full cart on her phone profile. Dev couldn't reach the quantity or Add To Cart controls with the keyboard. Lucía checked the peso arithmetic and found a one-cent difference.

I left Rosa, Dev and Lucía red on the board so I could find the purchase attempts that still needed work. The profiles stayed the same across the two rounds. Their model-chosen actions can vary from one run to the next.

The current repo has browser checks for the original, clean and patched shops. They check the three-telescope total without a model API. The November 11 run has its own saved results and spend ledger. The screenshots and results above are from November 4.

I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

#9810. Jikan shut down. Here's how I moved my anime app to AniList without rewriting every screen

In September 2026 the Jikan API, the unofficial MyAnimeList REST API that a lot of hobby anime apps were built on, went offline. My app, MyAnimeDex (a free anime tracker for iOS and Android), used it on almost every screen: search, anime details, seasonal charts, recommendations.

This is how I moved everything to the AniList GraphQL API without touching most of those screens, and the rate-limit bugs I hit on the way.

Screens imported one module, lib/jikan.ts, and used Jikan-shaped objects: mal_id, images.jpg.large_image_url, genres: [{ mal_id, name }] and so on. Rewriting the home screen, anime details, lists, onboarding, the dice picker and the recommendation service to AniList's shape at once would have broken things I couldn't easily test.

Instead lib/jikan.ts kept its exports and types, and started delegating to a new AniList service. A normalizer converts each AniList Media object into the old shape:

Two details mattered more than I expected:

AniList allows roughly 90 requests a minute, and less when the service is under load. My home screen fired a handful of parallel queries; the calendar fired one per day. On a busy day that was enough to hit HTTP 429, retry immediately, hit 429 again and loop.

The fix was a single entry point for every request:

After this, the rate-limit loops that had been my most persistent bug stopped.

Start with the facade, not the screens: one module that keeps your current data shape and talks to the new API behind it. Then put every request through one throttled client before you ship. In my case the rate-limit loops were harder to track down than the data mapping.

If you're maintaining a Jikan-based app and need to switch, I'm happy to answer questions in the comments.
