#9808. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9806. Importing Bandcamp ZIPs in a Flutter music player: streams, zip slip and Finder junk

People who still buy music mostly get it as a ZIP. Bandcamp, Qobuz and most download shops hand you one archive per album. My offline music player, Clickwheel, could only import loose audio files, so the first thing a new user had to do was find an unzip tool on their phone. That is a bad first minute.

So I added ZIP import. The diff was 469 lines across 13 files, and almost none of it was "call the unzip function". Here is what the rest was.

A FLAC album is easily several hundred megabytes. Reading it into a Uint8List on a phone is asking for an out-of-memory kill. The archive package (4.x) can decode from a file stream and write each entry straight to disk:

The function is synchronous on purpose. It is a static method that only takes two strings, so it can run in a background isolate with one line:

The click wheel keeps animating while the album unpacks, and the progress label ("Unpacking Some Artist - Some Album.zip") is set from the main isolate between archives.

A ZIP entry name is just a string chosen by whoever made the archive. ../../something is a valid name, and writing it blindly puts a file outside your target folder. This is the classic "zip slip" bug. My guard is small and boring:

On top of that, only files with a known audio extension are written at all. Cover scans, PDFs and .url files stay in the archive.

I work as a QA engineer, so this is the part I care about most. The archive package can also create ZIPs, which means the test builds its own hostile album in memory:

Five entries go in, two come out, and the last line checks that nothing landed one folder up. No fixture files in the repo, no binary blobs in code review.

Small decisions that took longer than the code:

On iOS most people download the ZIP in Safari and then tap Share. To appear there, the app declares the document types in Info.plist:

LSHandlerRank is Alternate on purpose. A music player should be offered for ZIP files, not become the default app for them.

The native side is a small Swift class that receives the URL, wraps the copy in startAccessingSecurityScopedResource() and moves the file into the media folder. The detail that bit me: on a cold start the file arrives before the Dart side is listening on the method channel. So the Swift side counts what came in, and Dart asks once at startup:

The unzip call is ten lines. The feature is everything around it: memory, the UI thread, hostile paths, Finder junk, cleanup, duplicates and cold starts. Writing the test list first would have given me the design for free.

Honest status: this is merged on the main branch and ships with the next store update. If you install the app today, ZIP import may not be in your build yet.

Clickwheel is an offline music player with a click wheel for your own MP3 and FLAC files, on iPhone and Android. You can turn the wheel in your browser: https://clickwheel-app.pages.dev/?ref=devto#rad

#9804. Building Smarter Inventory Systems: How RFID, IoT, and Real-Time Data Work Together

Inventory management might look like a simple process from the outside. A business receives products, stores them, and ships them when customers place orders.

But what happens when a warehouse handles thousands of items across multiple locations?

Keeping inventory records accurate becomes much more complicated.

Manual updates, delayed synchronization, misplaced products, and inconsistent records can create serious operational problems.

This is where modern technologies such as RFID, IoT, cloud computing, and real-time data processing become useful.

Let's explore how these technologies can work together to build smarter inventory systems.

Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) uses radio waves to identify tagged objects.

An RFID inventory system generally includes:

When a tagged item passes within the reader's effective range, its information can be captured and processed.

Unlike traditional barcode scanning, RFID can identify multiple tagged items without requiring individual visual scans.

For developers, this creates opportunities to automate inventory events and reduce repetitive manual operations.

RFID identifies items, while IoT can connect different devices and sensors to a centralized system.

For example, a warehouse might use connected devices to:

These devices can send information to backend systems through suitable communication protocols.

The result is improved visibility into what is happening inside the warehouse.

Collecting inventory information is only one part of the process.

The system also needs to process that information accurately.

A warehouse receives 50 tagged products. An RFID reader detects the tags, and the inventory system processes the incoming records.

The application can then update the stock quantity after validating the received items.

A simplified workflow might look like this:

Developers should also consider duplicate reads, network interruptions, data validation, and synchronization problems.

Without proper handling, the system may record the same inventory event more than once.

Modern inventory applications often need to communicate with other business systems.

For example, an inventory platform may integrate with:

Cloud-based architecture can make centralized data access and integration easier.

However, developers should pay attention to API security, access permissions, database consistency, and system reliability.

A well-designed inventory platform should not simply collect information. It should make that information useful to different business applications.

Artificial intelligence can add another layer of intelligence to inventory management.

With reliable historical data, machine learning models can help businesses:

For example, a demand forecasting model can analyze historical sales and seasonal patterns to estimate future inventory requirements.

Of course, the quality of predictions depends heavily on the quality and relevance of the available data.

Building a smart inventory system involves more than connecting readers and databases.

Some important technical challenges include:

Data accuracy: Incorrect or duplicated events can affect stock calculations.

Scalability: Systems should handle increasing numbers of products, devices, and transactions.

Integration: Different business applications may use different data formats and communication methods.

Security: Inventory information and connected devices need appropriate protection.

Connectivity: Network interruptions should not cause permanent data loss or inconsistent records.

Planning for these challenges early can make inventory applications more reliable.

The combination of RFID, IoT, cloud computing, and AI is creating new opportunities for inventory management.

For developers and technology teams, the interesting challenge is connecting physical warehouse activities with reliable digital systems.

A successful solution requires accurate data collection, thoughtful backend architecture, secure integrations, and practical user interfaces.

#9800. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

 

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.


Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Automatically Mint Your Content As NFTs



Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.


Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.


Alternatively, LimeWire acknowledges the importance of exclusivity. Creators can choose to share their posts exclusively with their premium subscribers. In doing so, the content remains a special offering solely for dedicated fans, creating an intimate and personalized experience within the LimeWire community. This flexibility in sharing options emphasizes LimeWire's commitment to empowering creators with choices in how they connect with their audience and distribute their digital creations.


After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.


If you make it public, anyone can discover your content and even trade the NFTs. If you choose to share the post only with your premium subscribers, it will be exclusive only to your fans.


Earn Revenue From Your Content

Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other users who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.


This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.


LMWR Tokens

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

Pricing Plans

You can sign up to LimeWire to use its AI tools for free. You will receive 10 credits to use and generate up to 20 AI images per day. You will also receive 50% of the ad revenue share. However, you will get more benefits with premium plans.

  • Pro plan: 

For $49 per month, you will get 5,000 credits per month, up to 10,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

  • Pro Plus plan: 

For $99 per month, you will get 11,250 credits per month, up to 2 2,500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

With all premium plans, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Conclusion

In conclusion, LimeWire emerges as a democratizing force in the creative landscape, providing an inclusive platform where anyone can unleash their artistic potential and effortlessly share their work. With the integration of AI, LimeWire eliminates traditional barriers, empowering designers, musicians, and artists to publish their creations and earn revenue with just a few clicks.


The ongoing commitment of LimeWire to innovation is evident in its plans to enhance generative AI tools with new features and models. The upcoming expansion to include music and video generation tools holds the promise of unlocking even more possibilities for creators. It sparks anticipation about the diverse and innovative ways in which artists will leverage these tools to produce and publish their own unique creations.


For those eager to explore, LimeWire's AI tools are readily accessible for free, providing an opportunity to experiment and delve into the world of generative art. As LimeWire continues to evolve, creators are encouraged to stay tuned for the launch of its forthcoming AI music and video generation tools, promising a future brimming with creative potential and endless artistic exploration

#9797. Your Crypto Exchange's Default Settings Could Change Your Tax Bill

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Sell one bitcoin from a balance of two on an exchange, and the confirmation shows a price and a quantity. It does not show which Bitcoin you sold.

That detail decides the tax bill. Take an illustrative investor who bought 1 BTC at $20,000 and another at $90,000, both more than a year ago, then sold 1 BTC at $110,000. If the older coin counts as sold, the gain is $90,000. If the newer one does, it is $20,000. Same trade, same day, a $70,000 difference in reported gain.

For two years the IRS has let U.S. investors settle that question in their own records. That arrangement ends on December 31, 2026. From the first sale of 2027, the choice has to go through the platform holding the coins, which raises a plain question: what can a customer actually tell the platform?

To find out, I read the public tax pages of 15 U.S. crypto platforms between October 27 and 29, 2026. Six of them do not state which coins they sell first.

The rule sits in Treasury Regulation 1.1012-1(j). When a broker holds your coins, and you do not identify specific units by the date and time of the sale, the earliest-acquired units in that account are treated as sold first. That is first-in, first-out, or FIFO, and it runs account by account. Coins at one exchange are not pooled with coins at another.

The IRS granted temporary relief in Notice 2025-7 and extended it in Notice 2026-20. Through December 31, 2026, an investor can identify units on their own books, no later than the date and time of each sale, or record a standing order there before selling. For 2026 sales, the units identified that way control for federal income tax purposes, even if the broker's report shows something else.

After that date, the notice says, taxpayers "may not rely" on the relief. Unless new guidance arrives, the identification has to reach the broker, either as a standing order or as a lot choice on the trade.

A quieter line in the same regulation matters too. When a broker offers only one way to identify units, that method "is treated as a standing order or instruction." The notice switches this off during the relief period for investors using it. From 2027 it applies, so on a single-method platform, the platform's method effectively becomes the customer's own instruction.

I used each platform's own help center, tax pages and terms, read against the IRS rules, and no third-party summaries.

"Not disclosed" means I found no statement on the platform's public pages. It does not mean the platform has no policy. Coinbase, for instance, names FIFO for its institutional Prime accounts but not for retail customers, and Webull's FIFO language covers securities.

Changing the method is a separate question:

Those settings have their own fine print. Kraken's has to be changed from a desktop device and applies only going forward. Coinbase says the method must be chosen before the trade settles, and a new choice covers open and future trades only.

2026 is the first year brokers must report cost basis on Form 1099-DA, and only for "covered" assets: coins bought on that platform on or after January 1, 2026, and kept there. Anything moved in from a wallet or another exchange is noncovered. For people who self-custody, that can be most of what they own.

What happens to those coins depends on where they land:

None of those is your actual cost. The same coin can show up as a blank, a $0 estimate or the price on the day it arrived, depending only on where you sent it.

Robinhood's ordering is no quirk. Treasury Regulation 1.6045-1 tells a broker with no customer instruction and no adequate transfer records to report units it did not acquire for the customer first, and only then work from the earliest date. Your own default is plain FIFO. So the form can list different units from the ones you must treat as sold, and a worked example in Regulation 1.1012-1 shows exactly that.

The form can be right and your return can still need different numbers, with the adjustment shown on Form 8949. That matters because the IRS gets a copy of the form. As attorney and CPA David Klasing explained in a HackerNoon interview on John Doe summonses, the agency has used those orders to spot mismatches between crypto activity and reported taxes. Form 1099-DA puts that data on a standard form for every customer.

Find your method and date it. Look up your platform's default, save the page and note the day you checked. If nothing is published, ask support and keep the written answer.

Identify lots before each 2026 sale, not after. The relief requires the identification no later than the date and time of the sale, so a spreadsheet filled in during January will not rescue December trades. Use something that pins down basis and holding period, such as the purchase date, time and price.

Decide your 2027 setup before your first January sale. If your platform has a setting, pick the method and screenshot it. If it offers lot picking, plan to choose on every order. HIFO is not automatically the better pick: the highest-cost lot may be short-term, and using it first leaves your low-basis coins for a later year. Run both numbers on your own lots.

Export everything now. An earlier HackerNoon piece on crypto tax myths pointed out that most reputable exchanges let you download your transactions into a spreadsheet. Do that for every account, including the ones you rarely open, and keep withdrawals and deposits so both sides of each transfer can be matched.

Add missing basis before forms are generated. The windows are short. Strike asks customers to finish their details before it generates forms in mid-February. Robinhood's cutoff for 2025 sales was January 14, 2026, with a warning that updates after January 7 could delay forms. Assume the next window will be just as tight.

One date to remember: December 31, 2026. It is the last day a lot choice on your own books can count, and Strike warns that its tax year follows UTC, so there the year ends at 7:00 p.m. ET. The next marker follows quickly. Forms are due to customers by February 16, 2027, because February 15 is Washington's Birthday, and those will be the first to carry basis.

The IRS has extended this relief once. Planning on a second extension is a gamble.

Platforms are also still catching up. Several help pages show the old $600 threshold for Form 1099-MISC, although the figure for 2026 is $2,000. So treat any table, this one included, as a snapshot. The full version, with the quote and source link for each platform, is in the study, and the data is archived on Zenodo under a CC BY 4.0 license.

Disclosure: This is general information, not tax advice, DYOR! The author is a Florida CPA who runs a crypto accounting practice.

#9796. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9794. O certificado ISO 42001 tem prazo de validade: o que acontece entre a emissão e o vencimento

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at iso42001.com.br

Boa parte das empresas que certificam a ISO 42001 trata a auditoria inicial como linha de chegada. Ela não é. O certificado dura três anos, e dentro desse prazo existe um calendário obrigatório de visitas que decide se ele continua valendo ou se vira papel vencido. Eu entendo essa escolha como auditor, não como quem vende certificação: um sistema de gestão é um conjunto de práticas que a empresa precisa continuar executando depois que o auditor vai embora, não um produto testado uma vez. A ISO 42001 certifica a prática contínua, e um ciclo com verificação anual é o jeito da norma confirmar isso.

A lógica do ciclo não nasce na norma de IA. Vem da ISO/IEC 17021-1:2015, que rege como qualquer organismo certificador conduz auditoria e certificação de sistema de gestão, seja de qualidade, de segurança da informação ou de IA. A cláusula 9.1.3.2 define a estrutura: auditoria inicial em dois estágios, manutenção no primeiro ano, manutenção no segundo ano, recertificação no terceiro ano, antes do certificado expirar. Quem ainda não passou pela certificação inicial encontra esse primeiro ciclo, com estágio 1, estágio 2 e custo, detalhado à parte. Este texto assume que o certificado já está em mãos e foca no que vem depois dele.

A manutenção é obrigatória pelo menos uma vez por ano civil, exceto no ano em que cai a recertificação. E a primeira precisa ocorrer em até 12 meses a partir da data da decisão de certificação, não da data em que a auditoria terminou. Isso importa na prática: se o organismo certificador demora para processar a decisão, o relógio da primeira manutenção já está correndo antes de a empresa perceber. O escopo é menor que o da auditoria inicial. O auditor não reavalia o Anexo A inteiro, cláusula por cláusula; ele amostra partes do sistema, confirma que as não conformidades da visita anterior foram corrigidas e verifica se a empresa continua operando o sistema de gestão de IA como declarado, não apenas como documentado. Isso inclui conferir se novos sistemas de IA entraram em produção desde a última visita e se foram incorporados ao inventário e à avaliação de impacto. É exatamente aqui que eu vejo o ponto escapar com frequência: a empresa certifica o parque de IA que tinha no ano 1 e esquece de atualizar o escopo quando um time novo adota uma ferramenta no ano 2. Sob a ISO/IEC 42006:2025, o tempo de qualquer visita é calculado pelo número e complexidade dos sistemas em escopo, não por uma tabela fixa de desconto. Uma empresa que adicionou sistemas de alto risco entre uma visita e outra pode ter uma manutenção mais longa do que o esperado, mesmo sendo "só" manutenção.

O organismo certificador primeiro registra a não conformidade de prazo. Se a empresa não agenda a visita dentro de uma margem definida pelo próprio organismo, o certificado é suspenso, o que já impede o uso dele em proposta, contrato ou due diligence de cliente. Se a situação continuar sem solução, a suspensão vira retirada, e a empresa perde o certificado por completo. A parte cara vem depois: uma empresa com certificado retirado não reativa com uma visita de manutenção atrasada. Ela precisa passar outra vez pela auditoria inicial completa, em dois estágios, como se nunca tivesse sido certificada. O atraso que parecia administrável, uma reunião remarcada, um auditor sem agenda disponível, termina custando o tempo e o valor de um processo de certificação inteiro, do zero.

No terceiro ano, a recertificação reavalia o sistema de gestão inteiro, nos mesmos moldes da auditoria inicial, mas com uma diferença de ponto de partida: o auditor já tem três anos de histórico para comparar, duas auditorias de manutenção, não conformidades anteriores e o registro de evolução do parque de sistemas de IA. Ele não está testando se o sistema existe, está testando se ele sobreviveu a três anos de operação real sem virar documento esquecido numa pasta. Vale tratar o ano da recertificação como o momento de revisar premissa, não só de reunir evidência. Se a empresa adotou tipos de sistema de IA que não existiam quando a política original foi escrita, por exemplo um modelo de linguagem usado para triagem de currículo que não fazia parte do escopo há três anos, a recertificação é o momento de atualizar política, inventário e avaliação de impacto de uma vez, em vez de corrigir aos poucos em cada manutenção seguinte.

Imagine uma empresa de crédito digital que certificou a ISO 42001 com dois sistemas de IA em escopo, ambos de avaliação de risco de crédito. Nos três anos seguintes, o time de produto lança um assistente de atendimento baseado em modelo de linguagem e um sistema de detecção de fraude, nenhum deles formalmente incluído no inventário. Na recertificação, o auditor encontra os dois sistemas novos em produção, sem avaliação de impacto registrada. Isso vira não conformidade maior e atrasa a emissão do novo certificado até a lacuna ser corrigida. Nada nesse cenário envolve má-fé. Envolve um inventário que parou no dia da certificação inicial e nunca mais foi atualizado, enquanto o produto seguia lançando coisa nova.

#9791. Data Extraction for AI Agents: 10 MCP Prompts for PDFs, Scans and Forms

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Your agent can read an invoice. What it can't do is show you where each number came from, or do the same thing reliably across 10,000 invoices.

Ask Claude Code or Codex to pull the total from a scanned PDF and you usually get one of three things: a guess, a value from the wrong table row, or a confident answer with no way to check where it came from. That's fine for a demo. It isn't fine when the number goes into an accounting system.

This post gives you 10 copy-paste prompts that let an agent read documents properly: pull fields from invoices, tables from statements and text from scans, each value with its source. The agent connects to a data extraction APIover the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Every prompt below was run with the live server connected, and the outputs shown are real.

I tested this on a tilted, noisy scan of a supplier invoice: an image with no text layer at all. Claude read it on its own and got the invoice date and the total right. When I asked where those values were, the best it could do was "top right, about 13% down the page" for the date, and "right side, about 55% down" for the total.

The extraction API returned the same values with evidence:

One caveat: a citation points to the source region, not always the exact word. The date's box is tight and covers the label and the value. The total's box covers the whole totals block, from subtotal to total. A review screen highlights that block, which is still far quicker to check than "about 55% down".

A PDF doesn't store "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores characters at coordinates. Everything a human sees has to be reconstructed: reading order, columns, table cells, which number belongs to which label. Scans are worse, because there's no text at all until OCR runs.

When a general-purpose model reads a PDF directly, four things tend to go wrong:

The fix is to give the agent a document data extraction tool that does the parsing and returns structured output with a source location for every value. The agent keeps doing what it's good at: deciding what to ask for and what to do with the answer.

The server is hosted, so there's nothing to install and no API key in a config file. You sign in once with OAuth.

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp

Then start a new session, run /mcp, choose nutrient, and select Authenticate.

codex mcp add nutrient --url https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp && codex mcp login nutrient

Claude app: Settings → Connectors → add a custom connector with https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp.

Full setup details are in the MCP server guide.

Each prompt is written the way you'd type it to your agent. Swap in your own file names.

When to use it: any time a number from a document goes into another system.

Extract vendor, invoice number, date, line items and total from invoice.pdf.

What came back: every field correct. Shortened, showing 2 of the 6 line items:

All 6 line items came back, including a −$169.00 credit for returned brackets. The total matches the invoice: $1,835.00 subtotal + $48.00 shipping + $114.91 tax = $1,997.91.

Every value comes with its page, a bounding box and a groundedness score. Here's the citation for the total, as returned:

You don't need to ask for locations; they come back anyway. My first version of this prompt ended with "Show the page and source location for each value." The server turned that into extra fields filled with descriptions like "Upper right, beside 'Invoice date'", which added nothing and caused review flags (see prompt 2).

Two more things to know. The field names are generated for each document: vendor and total here, not a fixed schema. And the output keeps what’s printed: line-item descriptions kept the invoice’s tax marker, as in “Anchor bolt M16 x 200 mm T”.

When to use it: before you import anything automatically.

For every value you extracted, flag anything with low confidence so I can review it before import.

What came back: one value flagged for review: the unit price on the −$169.00 credit line, with a groundedness score of 0.18. The value was correct. Every other field scored between 0.97 and 0.9997 and was marked ready to import.

That's the behavior you want from a review step: it leans towards asking a person. An earlier run, using my first version of prompt 1, came back with 14 flags, mostly on the extra "source location" fields that prompt created. It's a good reason to keep extraction prompts to the fields you need.

When to use it: before chunking documents for retrieval.

Parse report.pdf to Markdown, keeping tables and reading order, and save it as report.md.

What came back: clean headings, the abstract and introduction in order, and the results table intact (as an HTML table, which keeps merged cells). A chart even came back as a table. The test file was a three-page, two-column research paper, and reading order wasn't perfect:

Check the Markdown of a multi-column document before you index it. Single-column documents are much easier.

When to use it: contracts, faxes, anything that arrived as an image.

This is a scanned contract. Parse it with OCR and list the parties, the effective date and who signed.

What came back: the test file was a 3-page image-only scan, slightly tilted and noisy. Parsing took about 13 seconds and cost $0.054 ($0.018 a page). The answer:

Parties: Nexus Digital Solutions, LLC (Service Provider) and Bridgewater Logistics Partners, Inc. (Client)

Signed by: Elena V. Marchetti, Chief Executive Officer, and Derek L. Fontaine, Chief Operating Officer, both dated February 14, 2024

All correct. The noise left stray characters in the parsed text, such as "oo", "ve" and "fe" between two sections, and "Derek L. Fontaine t t" on the signature page. That's normal for scans. The agent's answer stayed clean, and the citations tell you which region to check if something looks off.

When to use it: statements, price lists, reports.

Pull every table from statement.pdf into JSON, then save each table as its own CSV file.

What came back: both tables, the account summary and all 7 transactions, saved as two CSV files. Shortened:

Empty debit and credit cells came back empty, not as zero, which matters if you sum the columns later. The closing balance matched the statement: $7,692.81.

When to use it: an inbox or upload folder with mixed file types.

Classify every file in ./inbox as invoice, receipt, contract or ID document, and move each file into a folder named after its type.

The server classifies; the agent moves the files. Run this one in Claude Code or Codex rather than a chat app.

When to use it: monthly invoice runs, batches of forms.

Extract the same fields from all invoices in ./invoices in one batch, and build one spreadsheet with a row per invoice.

What came back: three invoices from three different suppliers, each with a different layout. The server generated one 20-field schema and applied it to all three. A few columns from the spreadsheet:

All three totals are correct. On the Tidewell invoice, it took the balance due after a $1,500 retainer, not the $6,152.50 in fees.

Tip: run files of one kind together, and say how you want values formatted. Without that, our batch came back with "USD" on two invoices and "$" on the third, and three different date formats. Adding "Use ISO 4217 codes for currency and YYYY-MM-DD for dates" fixed all three. Two things to check after a run like this. A "$" with no country is the model's best guess: here it said USD, citing the supplier's Oregon address. And a field that doesn't fit the format can come back empty: one invoice listed three ship dates, and with the date rule that field came back blank.

When to use it: a new document type you haven't processed before.

Show me which fields you'd extract from claim.pdf before running the extraction.

What came back: 19 proposed fields for a property damage claim form, including claimant_name, policy_number, date_of_loss, type_of_loss and account_number. Each field comes with a rule. Every rule starts with "If no value is observed, return null rather than inventing a value", and then adds specifics. For example, the rule for police_or_fire_report_number is "including an explicit N/A; null if blank". The response said: "Nothing was extracted, billed or stored."

The list isn't fixed. An earlier run on a similar form proposed 21 fields. Edit the list until it has what you need, then use the same list for every file of that type.

When to use it: before sending a document to a vendor, a model, or a colleague who doesn't need the personal data.

Redact names, email addresses, phone numbers and bank account numbers in claim.pdf, then save a redacted copy.

What came back: the claimant's name, email, phone number and account number were removed, both in the form fields and in the free-text description. It also caught the name of a neighbour mentioned in the description. The text is gone from the file, not just covered by a black box. The policy number, address and routing number stayed, because the prompt didn't ask for them.

Two things to watch. The bank name was removed even though the prompt didn't ask for it. And thetyped signature "R. M. Okafor" was removed in one run and left in another. If something must go, name it in the prompt ("…and signatures"), and open the redacted copy before you send it.

When to use it: before you process a folder of documents.

Count the pages in ./invoices and estimate what extracting them will cost at $0.015 per page.

What came back: 3 invoices, 1 page each, so about $0.045. The agent counted the pages itself, locally, without sending anything to the server, so the estimate is free. The rate comes from your prompt. Extraction currently costs $0.015 per page, and parsing $0.009 or $0.018 depending on the mode. To see what you've actually used, check the Nutrient dashboard.

Start with prompt 1 on one real document from your own work, and open the cited regions to check them. Once you trust the output for that document type, move to batches.

The parsing mode decides most of the cost:

Extraction (prompts 1, 5 and 7) ran in understand mode, at $0.015 per page.

Parsing a document to Markdown (prompts 3 and 4) defaults to agentic mode, at $0.018 per page.

On the clean three-page research paper, I reran the parse in understand mode at $0.009 per page. The Markdown was nearly identical, at half the price, in 1.2 seconds.

Agentic mode is for messy scans and complex layouts. For clean digital PDFs, ask for understand mode and compare both on a sample before you process thousands of pages.

Finally, keep a person in the loop for anything that moves money or makes a decision. The citations and confidence scores are there so the review takes seconds, not so you can skip it.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

#9789. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

The digital landscape has evolved dramatically, and AI tools have become essential for creators who want to stay ahead of the curve. In this guide, I'll show you the top 10 AI tools that are revolutionizing content creation and making creators' lives easier.

Why You Need These AI Tools in 2025

#9784. Building a $0 Modern Data Platform: dbt, MotherDuck, and Automated CI/CD (Zero AWS Required)

Author: Fabrizio Perez Peralta Course: Business Intelligence Published on: [Dev.to / HashNode / Medium] Public Repository: GitHub Repository Link Live Dashboard: Streamlit Community Cloud Live App

In recent years, the Modern Data Stack (MDS) has revolutionized how organizations extract, transform, and analyze information. However, traditional implementations often come with a steep barrier to entry: enterprise data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift), paid managed orchestrators (Astronomer, Airflow clusters), and complex cloud infrastructure (AWS VPCs, IAM roles, S3 buckets). For small teams, startups, or students, these costs and operational overhead quickly become prohibitive.

The Question: Can we build a production-grade, automated Data Engineering pipeline using industry-standard tools (like dbt), deployed to a public SaaS provider, with zero infrastructure management and a monthly cloud bill of exactly $0.00?

The Answer: Yes. By combining MotherDuck (Serverless DuckDB in the cloud), dbt-core, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and Streamlit Community Cloud for business intelligence, we can create an end-to-end cloud data platform with high performance and zero cost.

In this article, I will walk you through the architecture, data modeling, automated deployment, and lessons learned from building this solution.

Our solution follows the classical Medallion Architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold), orchestrated via automation:

Before transforming data, we must ingest it. We created a lightweight Python script (scripts/extract_load.py) that queries public cryptocurrency and market indicators.

To guarantee that the pipeline never fails due to transient network glitches or public API rate limits, the script incorporates an automatic fallback mechanism:

Once raw data lands in raw.raw_crypto_market (the Bronze layer), we leverage dbt to clean, enrich, and model the data.

In the staging layer, we cast data types, standardize string formatting, and deduplicate records by keeping only the latest snapshot per asset:

In this layer, we derive actionable business intelligence metrics:

The final consumer layer adheres to dimensional modeling (star schema):

Data engineering without testing is just wishful thinking. In models/marts/schema.yml, we define rigorous assertions executed automatically by dbt test:

If any constraint fails (e.g., duplicate IDs or unexpected risk values), the CI/CD pipeline immediately stops, preventing corrupted data from reaching the serving layer.

To fulfill the requirement of automated deployment, we configured a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/pipeline.yml).

The pipeline runs on every code push and automatically every 12 hours:

By storing our MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN in GitHub Secrets, our automated runner can authenticate securely to the cloud data warehouse without hardcoding credentials.

Finally, to deliver value to decision-makers, we deployed a web dashboard on Streamlit Community Cloud (a public SaaS provider).

The dashboard connects directly to MotherDuck via read-only SQL queries and renders:

Because Streamlit Cloud is linked to the GitHub repository, any update pushed to main is instantly reflected in the live application.

Feel free to leave a comment, star the repository, or connect on LinkedIn if you have any questions or feedback!

#9782. The 12 best recipes to bake in October: It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make.

What do jobs, school, sports practices, and commuting have in common? They all prevent us from baking as much or as often as we’d like. But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Pumpkin Pie Spice
